I think I've pieced together that the judge had them sort their decks
so they could be matched against the decklist, and that people were
pissed off that they had a bad draw, and thought it was because the
deck had been sorted.

It doesn't matter how sorted your deck is. If it wasn't randomized
after you shuffled, then you are at fault, because it is your
responsibility to randomize your deck. Put it this way: if you arrange
your deck such that like cards are not next to each other, and then
shuffle lightly, you have not sufficiently randomized your deck - it
wouldn't be as obvious, but you would still be in violation. If your
shuffling is not sufficient to randomize when the deck is sorted, then
it wasn't sufficient to randomize even if the deck had been sequenced
in some other way.

There was at least one study done that indicated such, although I do not
have a link or other information handy. I have not checked Google;
perhaps it's right there on page 1.

The 'perfect' riffle, of course, is not actually a shuffle at all as it
does not leave any cards in an unknown position -- which means that the
results of the study are inherently suspect, as part of any experiment
is reproducibility. Random isn't reproducible, by definition, so one of
the few useful tests would be to use a truly random shuffling method to
sort the 52 cards, and then compare the results to 7 "imperfect riffles"
to see how much more of a pattern there tends to be from the riffles...
in other words, how many times you get results that were similar to a
prior result, compared to how many times you got that with the
true-random method. But even here there's an element of uncertainty
involved about the results, as your test for "similar results" is going
to, by necessity, be a bit weak.

In short, it's pretty hard to test "random". The literal definition is
that given a deck of 52 cards numbered 1 through 52 and any given
shuffling method, the chances that the cards come up ordered as:

1, 2, 3, ... 51, 52

... should be identical to the chances they come up:

52, 51, 50, ... 2, 1

... and the chances of being ordered in ALL other possible combinations.
Easy to brute-force test with dice ... not so easy to do with cards.

> Assuming there is math to show that 7 shuffles are sufficient to
> randomize a 52 card deck, I'd like to know how many shuffles are enough
> to randomize a 90 card deck.

Even assuming the study is accurate, it would take way more than 7, and
certainly more than players currently do.

> Also, I've seen a lot of players "shuffle" their decks by counting them
> out into 6* piles, and then stacking the piles. *Sometimes more or
> less than 6. Perhaps doing that is "better" randomization than
> shuffling?

Depends on whose point of view you're using. Many people believe it's
better randomization, and the owner of the deck will always tell you "I
get better shuffles this way."

From an objective view, it's not actually randomization at all; it's
intentional de-clumping, and as such I don't consider it to be shuffling
of any sort -- after someone does this, I expect to see them use some
form of actual shuffling on the deck. If they shuffle honestly, by the
definition of random above, it won't matter what order the cards went
into the deck.

> I'm curious about this and I'm not sure how to do the math. I might do
> some internet searching on it later, but if anyone already knows,
> please post here.

Well, you really don't need the math. What you do need to know is:

-- 90 cards are significantly more difficult to shuffle, PHYSICALLY,
than 52 cards. In Vegas, dealers do a "rough mix" prior to all
shuffling; the best way to understand THAT is to watch it on your local
Texas Hold 'Em TV program. It is the best randomization they have
available to them; the several riffle shuffles they do afterwards is
simply icing on the cake.

-- Vegas dealers have it easier than V:TES players. Vegas dealers only
really need people to not be able to predict the order the cards will
come in, and they rarely use the entire deck. V:TES players ALSO need
to have no significant bias in their deck either towards or against
clumping; if you have six Blood Dolls, it should be equally likely for
them to be all in the top 15 cards, spread out through the deck evenly,
or all in the bottom 15 -- and because V:TES players can potentially use
the entire deck, it actually matters a lot more from the viewpoint of
correct randomization *AND* from gameplay; while many decks benefit more
from having an even distribution and no cards of the same type next to
each other, others such as Giovanni powerbleed will do much better
drawing up all their Governs early, and all their Conditionings and
Foreshadowings in the later part of the deck, when the hammer really
needs to be dropped *AFTER* the block decision is made.

-- Most V:TES players will never rough-mix their cards, out of fear of
damaging the condition. Combined with their inability to shuffle a
90-card deck properly, the play of the game suffers as a result...
certainly so for those who choose not to separate their cards
beforehand, as they will be more likely to clump up. I personally note
that I get more "expected" results out of a deck after it's been played
a few times -- this is undoubtedly because combos end up next to each
other in the ash heap, and even though I do put some effort into making
my shuffle random, even my hands aren't good enough to split up EVERY
combo and create a truly random order (although remember, the
possibility must exist that some combos ARE together in the perfect play
order as well).

-- The above is not an endorsement of table-shuffling, however, as that
action biases the output of the deck in exactly the OPPOSITE fashion
from not separating cards; it makes the output much more unlikely to be
clumped than it normally would be in a random shuffle. This is just as
bad, and in fact slightly worse since it gives the separators an
advantage over the non-separators... if the non-separators' deck is
ordered in clumps, that is. If it's not ordered (say, it's been played
a bunch), the results will be unpredictable as to who will get more
"clumping", as the initial order is unknown.

(breathes)

...AS FAR AS the whole getting-a-free-ticket thing goes, which ruling
exactly do I need to disagree with to collect? I can be bribed. :D

--
Derek

This is the default recommendation. It is not "only escalated" in such
a fashion in the real world.

The rules make quite clear, however, that a judge can award a repeated
offence without escalation or that they can skip to a higher penalty.

The recommended penalty for the first offense is listed in the
"Penalty" portion of each infraction. For the second offense of
the same infraction, the next highest penalty is recommended.

In a given situation without further explanation or clarification, a
player does NOT know how you are going to apply the next penalty and the
rules do not allow for them to know. Guess, perhaps, but they can never
know.

One reason behind this is obvious. If a player knows they can get away
with something due to a rigid application of the rules, they can save up
their warning for a particularly egregious breach of the rules. As the
rules stand, players cannot do that because the judge can respond
appropriately, not mechanically.

x5m...@gmx.de writes:
>If a wrong decklist is usually not indicating that a player wanted to
>cheat, why do we always punish them with a disqualification.

There are two reasons that spring to my mind, principally.

First of all, it's extremely difficult to tell the difference between an
honest mistake and intentional cheating, in this instance. All you have
to go on is the player's say-so. With - for example - an in-game form
of cheating, you may have witnessed it yourself or you may be able to
ask other players for their opinions of what happened.

Secondly, unlike a situation where a player makes an honest mistake
about something on the spur of the moment (e.g. mis-interprets a card

In the former case, you've applyed your Judgement rationally and fairly.
In the latter, you've abandoned the use of your Judgement, in favor of
saying that you have no way of Judging if the player's infraction is
accidental of intentional. I guess this is my problem with the use of the
Judge's guidelines in this fashion. If you are a Judge, make the call. One
should either have confidence enough in one's Judgely evaluation of the
person and the circumstances to call the offending player a Cheater (and
apply penalties under section 163) if they believe that he is
misrepresenting his deck, _or_ have the confidence in their Judgement of the
player and the circumtances to call the error unintentional, and correct the
issue with a deck or decklist adjustment and a formal warning.
But no judge should shy away from Judging by saying "we'll _I_ have no way
of knowing, so therefore I'll just apply this default penalty", using the
Penlty Guide as a shield for the inability to arrive at an affirmative
conclusion. That strikes me as simply a cop-out from actually Judging the
situation. Be a Judge. Make the call.

As for me, to arrive at the conclusion that a person is cheating by way of
altering his deck mid-game, I would require affirmative evidence of such,
and an error on a decklist is insufficient evidence to draw that conclusion,
since errors (the majority of errors, in fact) may be arrived at by a myriad
of ways not related to cheating.

Note also, given the mode and frequency of decklist verification used in
the EC (check decks of finalists against their decklists before entering the
finals, no checks of those same decks before), the default penalty (Game
Loss) is essentially no different to the player at fault than a Full
Disqualification. (quite possibly its Worse, since the party you penalize
will have basically wasted three preliminary rounds and six hours of their
own time in getting to that finals position). _That_ is a implementation of
decklist checking which was entirely established by the administrator(s) of
the event, and is lacking IMO. If I was going to apply a Game Loss to a
finalist of a major event, then I'd want a baseline deck check of that
player in place *before the first round*, so as to be able to verify that
the deck actually _had_ been altered over the course of the event. If I
lacked that baseline check, I'd need more evidence of foul play to indicate
that a Game Loss (again, equivalent to a Full Disqualification, in this
circumstance) was the appropriate penalty.

> sure everybody has those points. I'm just not sure that using a
> completely

A Straw Man, Daneel, and you're better than that... Look, I'm not getting
down on you or anyone else in particular here. It seems that this
interpretation of decklists is pretty comprehensively applied to the whole
of the European community. Fine, IMO it detracts from the game
tremendously, but its your event. To take arguments against this _specific_
means of implementing decklist checks as meaning that _any_ adjustment from
a default penalty is somehow an indication of a rogue Judge establishing his
own guidelines, is fallacy.

The greater problem is with how the deck-checking method has been set up,
anyways, as it offers no baseline for the Judge to make a clear call as to
whether the decklist has a clerical error, or if the player has altered the
deck mid-tournament. I think if this shortcoming of the decklist-checking
methodology were addressed, there would be no issue for anyone with how the
penalties were applied...

I thought I did, but then I did some quick experiments and now I think I
don't.

My theory before was that you should use a number of piles that is prime
relative to the number of cards in your library, on the idea that a number
of piles that factors evenly into the size of your library, if you always
stack the piles back together in the same order as you placed them down,
would more quickly return to the original pre-shuffling order.

My idea that prime numbers of piles avoided this problem appears to be
entirely wrong. Looking at a twenty-card library, it seems to take 9
pile-shuffles (see Appendix A for details) to return to the original order
using either 4 or 5 piles; 18 pile-shuffles to return to the original order
with 2 or 10 piles; but only 4 pile-shuffles to return to the original order
with either 3 or 7 piles. I *really* don't know why this is, but then my
matrix math isn't all that good. (I tried 6 piles, and got tired of typing
(after 58 'shuffles') without reaching a point where the order repeats
exactly, but there are some dramatic repeating patterns in there
nonetheless - notably that the seventeenth card (damn you letter Q!) is
*always* in the same place.)

I think now that you are very much right to try to deal your cards randomly
onto the piles, and that any deterministic pile-shuffle must be pretty
severely flawed as a randomizing method. (One obvious problem is that your
top and bottom cards always stay on the top and bottom if your cards deal
out evenly into non-random piles, but there seem to be lots of patterns
along the way besides that one.)

As a side-note, a pile shuffle with two piles is exactly the same as a
"perfect" riffle shuffle (and has the same problems as a "perfect" riffle
shuffle would).

"6.3. Constructed Deck Registration

The head judge or tournament organizer may require players to register
their decks upon arrival at a tournament. Registration records the
original composition of each deck. Once a tournament official receives
a player's decklist, the deck may not be altered. Failure to properly
register a deck will result in the head judge applying the appropriate
provisions of the V:EKN Penalty Guidelines. The V:EKN recommends that

each round."

judge, and there's a _lot_ of ways you can implement decklists poorly.

make use of decklists (particualrly to check contents for finalists),

their decks sorted to correspond with their decklist when submitting
them for review, to speed the review process (a written decklist with
sorted contents alongside would take less than one minute to review).

their lists before the finals, and can apply a more specific ruling
regarding altered deck contents.

of detail in section 6.3 of the Tournament Rules, than I am with
anything found in the Penalty Guidelines.
